study.title: 2 Chronicles 30 - The Passover restored by Hezekiah
study.overview: The chapter shows Hezekiah leading Judah and also the remains of the ancient northern kingdom to a renewed celebration of the Passover in Jerusalem. The narrative highlights three axes: invitation to conversion, purification of worship and community joy before God's mercy. Even with delay in the calendar and with much ritual fragility, the king acts to gather the people to the Lord, and God responds with acceptance, healing and great joy.

outline.title: Invitation to Israel and Judah to return to the Lord
outline.explanation: Hezekiah send letters to all Israel and Judah, inviting Ephraim and Manasseh to Jerusalem to the passover. The decision to celebrate in the second month appears as a pastoral and liturgical solution in the face of the lack of sanctified priests and the dispersion of the people. The call appeals to the covenant with the parents, calling the people to repentance and the restoration of communion with God.

outline.title: Called to repentance and different answers
outline.explanation: The messages remind the failure of the ancestors, ask that the people not harden their hearts and promise mercy to those who turn to the Lord. The reaction is mixed: many scoff, but some humiliate themselves. In Judah, the narrative attributes to God himself the disposition of the heart to obey the real word according to the word of the Lord.

outline.title: Purification, sacrifice and divine acceptance
outline.explanation: The crowd gathers, removes idolatrous altars and celebrates the Passover in the second month. There are irregularities, because many were not cleansed, but Hezekiah intersects for them and asks that God accepts everyone who sought the Lord sincerely. The text states that the Lord heard the prayer and healed the people.

outline.title: Prolonged joy and final blessing
outline.explanation: The feast of unleavened bread is marked by continuous praise, peace offerings and gratitude. The people decide to add seven more days, supported by the generosity of the king and princes. The chapter culminates in great joy, without parallel from the days of Solomon, and at the close the priests and Levites bless the people, with prayer coming to heaven.

study.context: The chapter depicts a reformation of the cult in Jerusalem under Hezekiah, at the beginning of his reign. The text mentions Israel and Judah, as well as the tribes of the ancient northern kingdom, showing that the concern of the narrator is not only with Judah, but with the meeting of the covenant people. The notes indicate that the northern kingdom had already been affected by the Assyrian conquest and the dispersion of its inhabitants, which helps to understand why the convocation finds both mockery and some converts.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes that true restoration begins with return to the Lord, not only with external reorganization. The Passover functions as a memory of liberation and as a sign of renewal of the covenant. The celebration in the second month shows that God's mercy welcomes the sincere pursuit when the situation prevents ideal observance. Still, the text does not relativize holiness: there is purification, removal of idols, priestly order and intercession. Hezekiah's prayer is central: God can receive imperfect people when there is a heart prepared to seek him. The result is holy joy, communion and blessing, showing that repentance, worship and mercy walk together.

scholarViews.insight: The celebration of the Passover shows the chronicler's concern with the unity of Israel, with the spiritual preparation of the people and the restoration guided by what was established in the dedication of the temple.
The best preparation for the Passover was to remove the idolatrous altars; before the feast, they threw away the old sin.
Hezekiah celebrating in the second month was necessary because the purification of the temple was not completed in his own time, and the law already provided for this postponement in certain cases.

questions: What in the chapter shows that God values both the sincerity of the heart and the order of worship?
How does the mixed reaction of the people before the invitation of Hezekiah confronts our way of responding to the Word of God?
What idols or habits need to be removed today for worship to be more whole and joyful?
study.practice: The chapter calls the church and every believer to turn to the Lord with concrete repentance, to remove everything that is incumbent with worship, and to treat communion with God as something precious and restorative. The practice today includes examining the heart, abandoning visible and invisible idols, seeking the gathering of God's people with reverence and joy, and trusting that the Lord welcomes those who sincerely seek it, even if it comes with weaknesses.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not inform complete details of how each tribe answered, nor does it clarify all the legal aspects of the celebration in the second month beyond what the narrative itself states. The notes provided also do not allow to safely develop exact dates, geography beyond the text, nor historical reconstructions beyond the mention of the Assyrian conquest and the dispersion of part of the old northern kingdom.
